Magnesium helps your body activate and metabolize vitamin D.

This may explain why magnesium intake from food, supplements, or both, has been associated with lower odds of vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency.

Vitamin D from sunlight, food, or supplements needs to undergo conversions in the liver and kidneys to become its active hormone form, calcitriol. Magnesium supports the enzymes involved in this process, and enzymes that break vitamin D down.

Magnesium also supports parathyroid hormone secretion and action, which helps regulate vitamin D activation and calcium balance.

Nearly half of Americans get less magnesium from food and beverages than their estimated requirements. If you're paying attention to your vitamin D intake, your magnesium intake deserves attention, too.

BEFORE AGREEING TO A STATIN, ASK WHAT YOUR OVERALL RISK IS

If your doctor recommends a statin because of your LDL, ask what your overall heart risk is and whether a calcium scan would help make the decision.

But know which test you're discussing.

A coronary calcium scan measures calcified plaque. It doesn't use injected contrast. It cannot show all the soft plaque or tell you how narrow an artery is.

A coronary CT angiogram uses injected contrast to look at plaque and artery narrowing. It's a different test for a different clinical question.

A calcium score of zero is reassuring. It is not proof that you have no plaque, and it doesn't automatically mean you don't need treatment.

Neither scan is something everybody needs. Ask what the result would change about your care before buying another test.

One of the simplest ways to support your sleep starts in the morning - get outside into bright light for 10-15 minutes, minimum.

Light reaching your eyes helps synchronize the master clock in your brain. That clock helps coordinate daily rhythms throughout your body, including hormone release, metabolism, and the timing of sleep.

Cortisol is part of that rhythm. It gets a bad reputation because we associate it with stress, but its normal morning rise helps prepare you to wake up and become active.

Your body also needs a clear signal for when the day ends, so melatonin can rise and help prepare you for sleep.

Give that system a consistent schedule by waking up around the same time each day, getting outdoor light soon after waking when daylight is available, and keeping lights dimmer as bedtime approaches.

I was a great meat-eater. For years I believed I could not live without it. My health was poor—I fainted easily, felt weak and dizzy between meals—and a piece of flesh seemed the only thing that restored my strength. I thought it indispensable.

Then, on June 6, 1863, the Lord gave me a comprehensive vision on health reform. He showed me that the diet of flesh foods was not His original plan for man, that it was injurious to body and soul, and that His commandment-keeping people were to receive a reform diet. 

Disease and suffering would be lessened as they accepted it. The light was clear: eating the flesh of dead animals animalizes the system, strengthens the lower passions, beclouds the intellect, and corrupts the blood. Animals themselves were increasingly diseased—filled with tuberculosis, cancer, and parasites—and those who ate them took those diseases into their own bodies. Cancers, tumors, and inflammatory diseases were largely the result of this gross living.

I acted at once. Meat was cut from my table. I wrote and spoke the counsel: “Flesh meat is not necessary for health or strength.” The simple grains, fruits, and vegetables contain all the nutritive properties needed to make good blood. God permitted animal food after the Flood in part to shorten the lives of a corrupt race, but it was never the best food. In a land of abundance, there is no need to live on corpses.

I was careful. I never made it a test of fellowship. I said plainly that I would not declare no one should ever taste meat under any circumstances, for that would be carrying matters to extremes. Yet the principle stood: God’s people were to take a firm stand against meat-eating for their spiritual and physical good. 

Our sanitariums and medical institutions were to educate on this question. The Battle Creek Sanitarium, later Loma Linda, and the whole health work grew from that light. Physicians and workers trained there carried the message outward.

That counsel shaped the Seventh-day Adventist health system. The Adventist Health Studies that followed—large, long-term observations of our people—have been widely cited in discussions of plant-based diets, longevity, and chronic disease. Loma Linda itself became known as one of the “Blue Zones.” 

What began as a vision in 1863 entered the broader conversation about nutrition, fiber, and the supposed superiority of a non-flesh diet. The light given then still stands in our institutions and in the research they produced.

Lakshmi’s hands tell the rest of the story.
In the morning I walk to the shed near Kollam. The floor is already covered with roasted nuts. I squat the way my mother taught me, knees bent, back rounded, and begin. One shell, then the next. The wooden tool or the cutter cracks them open. That is when the oil comes.

The skin thickens and cracks. My nails pit. I rub ash on my hands before I start, the way everyone does. It helps a little. Gloves would slow me down, and we are paid by the kilo, not by the hour. If I shell or peel only six or seven kilos, the money is not enough. On a good day I manage ten or twelve. Many days the factory has fewer nuts and we are sent home early.

By afternoon my back is locked and my knees throb. The pain in my wrists and fingers does not stop when I stand up. At home I wash my hands again and again, but the stain stays. The burning can continue into the night. I cook rice, look after my mother, and try to sleep on my side so my back does not seize.

Some months we get only ten or twelve days of work. The piece rate has never been high. After bus fare and food there is little left. When the pain gets bad I go to the government hospital if I can. They give tablets. The dark marks on my hands do not go away.

I know other women who have the same hands as me. We sit in rows, cracking shells, peeling kernels, grading them. The smoke from the roasting and the dust make some of us cough. Our backs and knees grow worse every year. This is the work that is here. I started when I was young. My mother did it before me. My daughters will not, if I can help it.

People far away buy the nuts I peel. They blend them into milk, or press them into cheese, or use them in creamy sauces. They call these foods kind and clean. They say no animal suffered. Before insulin became widely available in the early 1920s, treating diabetes was a grim race against starvation and ketoacidosis. 

At the University of Michigan, Dr. Louis Harry Newburgh (1883–1956) developed a rigorous, high-fat, low-carbohydrate dietary approach that offered one of the more effective medical options of the era for managing severe diabetes.

Newburgh, a physiologist and clinician at Michigan, built on the work of earlier figures such as Frederick Allen (who used starvation diets) and Elliot Joslin. He argued that the key was not merely restricting calories or carbohydrates, but providing enough fat-derived calories to spare body protein while keeping carbohydrate intake extremely low—often under 20–30 grams per day. 

Patients were hospitalized and closely monitored. Their diets typically consisted of:
•  Very limited carbohydrate (often from carefully measured vegetables or a small amount of milk)
•  Generous amounts of fat (butter, cream, olive oil, fatty meats)
•  Moderate protein

The goal was to keep the patient in a mild state of ketosis while preventing the protein wasting and extreme emaciation of pure starvation regimens. Newburgh published detailed metabolic balance studies showing that many patients could maintain weight, clear sugar from their urine, and avoid the rapid decline seen with less structured approaches. Some of his more successful patients lived for years on these diets before insulin became available.

His work was part of a broader Michigan school of diabetes care that emphasized precise measurement, metabolic studies, and individualized diets rather than a one-size-fits-all starvation protocol. When insulin arrived (Banting and Best’s discovery in 1921, with clinical use expanding rapidly after 1922–23), Newburgh and his colleagues quickly integrated it. The dietary foundation he had developed proved useful even after insulin, as many physicians continued to use controlled low-carbohydrate diets alongside the new hormone.

Newburgh’s contributions
are sometimes overshadowed by the drama of insulin’s discovery, but in the years immediately before and just after insulin’s introduction, his measured high-fat approach represented one of the more scientifically grounded and relatively humane medical strategies available for people with severe diabetes. His papers from the 1920s remain interesting historical documents of metabolic medicine in the pre-insulin and early-insulin era.

The boy slips his hands into the gloves and must keep them on for about 10 minutes (sometimes described as longer). Showing pain or weakness is discouraged if he hopes to be seen as strong enough for leadership. Afterward his hands and arms may be swollen and temporarily paralyzed. The effects can linger for a day or more. 
This is not a one-time test. To complete the initiation he must repeat the ritual roughly 20 times, spread over months or even years. Only then is he considered a full man in the eyes of the community. 
Meaning
In Sateré-Mawé belief the ordeal builds physical and mental strength, proves courage, and functions almost like a spiritual “vaccine” that protects against illness and makes a better hunter and protector of the people and forest. A man who has not undergone it is sometimes viewed as unlucky or incomplete. Women participate in supporting roles (gathering materials, preparing drinks such as guaraná-based çapó), but the glove itself is for the boys. 
The ritual has been documented by anthropologists, National Geographic, and others (including adventurer Steve Backshall), and it continues today as a living tradition tied to cultural identity and the defense of ancestral lands.

It is an extreme, voluntary test of endurance rooted in a specific Amazonian culture—not a universal Indigenous practice. The pain is real and severe, but participants view it as transformative.

Misdiagnosed as Type 2 Diabetes? About 1 in 10 are!

Diabetes in adults isn't always type 2. Some people diagnosed with type 2 actually have LADA, latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, sometimes called type 1.5. Their immune system is slowly destroying the cells that make insulin.

This matters because no amount of metformin, other type 2 pills, or strict low-carb eating will bring their A1c to normal or stop the damage. They need insulin.

How common is each one? According to the CDC, about 90 to 95% of Americans with diabetes have type 2. LADA is much less common, but it's not rare. In a European study of 6,156 adults diagnosed with diabetes between ages 30 and 70, 9.7% had LADA. That's close to 1 in 10. In the UK Prospective Diabetes Study, 34% of people diagnosed with "type 2" between ages 25 and 34 had GAD antibodies, and 84% of those antibody-positive patients needed insulin within 6 years, compared with 14% of those without antibodies.

Here's how the mistake happens. An adult walks in with high blood sugar. Nine times out of ten that's type 2, so a lazy doctor writes "type 2," prescribes metformin, and never orders a C-peptide, insulin or antibody test. LADA comes on slowly, so at first it looks exactly like type 2, and the pills may even work for a while. When the sugars climb anyway, the patient gets blamed for not trying hard enough, and more pills get added. Meanwhile the pancreas keeps losing insulin-making cells, the high blood sugar keeps doing damage, and some people end up in the hospital with DKA before anyone checks.

Ask your doctor about LADA if:

1. Your blood sugar or A1c stays high even though you eat strict low-carb/keto/carnivore

2. You're losing weight without trying

3. You're thin or normal weight

4. You or a close family member has another autoimmune disease, like Hashimoto's thyroiditis

5. You were diagnosed younger than most people with type 2

Ask for these three tests:

1. C-peptide

2. Fasting serum insulin

3. GAD antibodies

A low C-peptide and low insulin with high blood sugar tells you your pancreas isn't making enough insulin. Positive GAD antibodies tell you why.

If it turns out you have LADA, low-carb still matters. Eating proper human food means you need much less insulin, your blood sugar stays steadier, and you have fewer lows. But it can't replace the insulin your body can no longer make.

If your numbers won't come down no matter how well you eat, it's not your fault. Get tested.

In the forests of the Brazilian and Venezuelan Amazon, the Yanomami still hunt and eat monkeys even when fruit trees are heavy with food.
The canopy around their villages is full of palms, figs, and other fruiting trees. People gather and eat those fruits, and they grow plantains and manioc in gardens. Yet meat—especially monkey meat—remains highly valued. Spider monkeys (Ateles belzebuth) are among the preferred game. Hunters say the meat tastes good, particularly when the animals are fat after feeding on seasonal fruits. Howler monkeys, peccaries, and birds are also taken. Large monkeys are relatively easy to locate because they travel in noisy groups, and their size makes the effort worthwhile. 
Men leave the village with bows, arrows, or (increasingly) guns. When they return with spider monkeys, the animals are often tied into a seated position, smoked or roasted, and shared. On big feasts tied to the peach-palm harvest, hunters have returned with dozens of spider monkeys alongside other game. Monkeys also appear in Yanomami mythology, technology, and adornment; some groups were historically called “monkey eaters” by outsiders because the practice was so characteristic. 
The same pattern appears among other Amazonian peoples. The Waorani (Huaorani) of Ecuador hunt large-bodied primates with blowguns and share the meat widely between households. The Shipibo of Peru list woolly and spider monkeys among preferred foods. Across the region, groups deliberately hunt monkeys when fruit is abundant precisely because that is when the animals are fattest. Plant foods and fish form the bulk of many diets by weight, but meat carries special cultural weight—status, sharing obligations, and a distinct sense of satisfaction that fruit alone does not provide.
This is not a matter of scarcity. The forests are productive in fruit, yet the preference for animal protein, fat, and the social value of hunting persists. Different groups maintain different taboos (some avoid tapir or deer while favoring monkey; neighbors reverse the pattern), using food choices partly as a way to mark identity. The result is that monkeys continue to be hunted and eaten in places surrounded by fruit.

The practice continues today in many remote communities, though firearms and population pressure have reduced some primate populations. Meat from monkeys and other game remains a central part of subsistence and culture for these groups.

When doctors first started writing about “mucous colitis” and “irritable colon” in the 1800s, they blamed nerves, hysteria, and spasm.
Osler (1892) described mucus casts, colicky pain, and depressed patients. Earlier writers noted the strange pattern of constipation one day and diarrhea the next. Food was treated as a treatment lever (high-fiber or low-residue diets), not the root cause.
But look at the timeline.
That was exactly when refined sugar went from a luxury to a daily staple—jumping from a few pounds per person per year to nearly 90 pounds in Britain by 1900. Cheap white flour from industrial roller mills replaced coarser whole-grain breads at the same time. Tea, jam, confectionery, and white bread flooded ordinary diets.
The pioneers of the condition didn’t connect the dots to the new food environment. Later researchers (Burkitt, Cleave, Painter) did—linking the rise of refined carbohydrates and the drop in cereal fiber to the wave of Western bowel disorders.
The symptoms were recognized. The dietary shift was happening in plain sight. The connection took another century.
